title: Job 32:6–22
context: Job 32:6–22 begins Elihu’s speech, and Elihu is the speaker from 32:6 through the end of chapter 33. He explains that he is young and held back out of respect for age (32:6–7), but that “there is a spirit in man, and the Spirit of the Almighty gives them understanding” (32:8); the word rendered spirit can also mean breath. Readers differ on whether Elihu is claiming a special inspiration for himself or appealing to the understanding God gives to every person regardless of age, and the verse can be read either way. He says that age does not guarantee wisdom (32:9), that he listened carefully but none of the three convinced Job (32:11–12), and he warns them against concluding that only God can refute Job (32:13). He describes himself as full of words, like new wineskins ready to burst (32:18–19), and promises to show no partiality or flattery (32:21–22). Some readers hear sincerity and courage in this preface, while others hear youthful self-importance; many hear something of both. These notes leave Elihu’s standing unresolved, as described in the introduction to the chapter.

verses.text: Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered, “I am young, and you are very old. Therefore I held back, and didn’t dare show you my opinion.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu begins, “I am young, and you are very old. Therefore I held back”. Arminian readers note Elihu’s courtesy in acknowledging his youth and his hesitance to speak, and they see a young person stepping forward because the older voices have left something important unsaid.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu frames his intervention carefully, honoring the elders while preparing to correct them. They observe that readers differ on whether this preface shows genuine humility or a show of modesty before a long speech, and they leave the question open.

verses.text: I said, ‘Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom.’
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says he thought, “Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom.” Arminian readers note that this expresses the common expectation of the wisdom tradition, which Bildad also voiced in appealing to past generations (8:8–10), and that Elihu now qualifies it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the saying is true as a general rule, since experience often brings wisdom, and they treat it as shared ground. They observe that Elihu’s point is not to despise age but to deny that age alone guarantees understanding of God’s ways.

verses.text: But there is a spirit in man, and the Spirit of the Almighty gives them understanding.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “But there is a spirit in man, and the Spirit of the Almighty gives them understanding.” Arminian readers note that the word rendered spirit can also mean breath, and they often read the verse as saying that God gives understanding to every person, not only to the aged.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some take the verse as Elihu’s claim to a special inspiration, while others read it as a general statement about God-given understanding. They hold the readings open and observe that, whichever is meant, the claim itself must be weighed by the rest of the book.

verses.text: It is not the great who are wise, nor the aged who understand justice.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “It is not the great who are wise, nor the aged who understand justice.” Arminian readers note that the wisdom books also warn against assuming that status or age bring insight, and they see the verse as opening space for a younger voice to be heard on its merits.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the statement is true as a caution, while observing that Elihu applies it in his own favor. They read it as a reminder that wisdom comes from God and is not guaranteed by rank, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: Therefore I said, ‘Listen to me; I also will show my opinion.’
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “Listen to me; I also will show my opinion.” Arminian readers note that Elihu presents his contribution as one opinion among others, at least in form, and they see a willingness to enter the conversation rather than to pronounce from above.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase I also will show my opinion recurs in the speech (32:17), and that readers have heard in the repetition either earnest eagerness or a certain self-importance. They hold such readings of Elihu’s tone loosely and without a verdict.

verses.text: “Behold, I waited for your words, and I listened for your reasoning, while you searched out what to say.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says he waited for their words and listened for their reasoning while they searched out what to say. Arminian readers note that Elihu presents himself as an attentive listener, which contrasts with the friends’ quickness to judge, and they see the verse as commending patient listening.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu emphasizes his careful attention as the basis for his right to speak. They observe that he has heard the whole debate, and they read the verse as preparing for his claim that none of the three answered Job’s words adequately.

verses.text: Yes, I gave you my full attention, but there was no one who convinced Job, or who answered his words, among you.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says that none of the friends convinced Job or answered his words. Arminian readers note that this judgment agrees with what the reader has seen in the dialogue, and they see Elihu identifying the friends’ failure to engage Job’s actual complaints about God and his suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu’s assessment of the friends is largely accurate, and that the LORD later says the friends did not speak rightly of him (42:7). They observe that Elihu’s agreement with that later verdict on the friends does not by itself establish his own standing.

verses.text: Beware lest you say, ‘We have found wisdom. God may refute him, not man;’
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu warns the friends not to say, “We have found wisdom. God may refute him, not man;” Arminian readers note that Elihu objects to the friends giving up on reasoning with Job and leaving him to God, and they see him taking responsibility for answering a fellow human being.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse may criticize the friends for claiming wisdom while abandoning the argument. They observe the irony that God does in fact answer Job (38:1), and they leave open how Elihu’s own speech relates to the LORD’s later answer.

verses.text: for he has not directed his words against me; neither will I answer him with your speeches.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says Job has not directed his words against him, and he will not answer Job with the friends’ speeches. Arminian readers note that Elihu claims to bring a fresh approach rather than repeating the three, and they leave it to readers to judge how far his arguments are new.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu distances himself from the friends’ arguments, though some readers think his later speeches repeat much of what they said. They hold that question open and read the verse as Elihu’s stated intention rather than the narrator’s assessment.

verses.text: “They are amazed. They answer no more. They don’t have a word to say.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says of the friends, “They are amazed. They answer no more. They don’t have a word to say.” Arminian readers note that the friends’ silence is the point of departure for Elihu’s speech, and they see it as confirming that the cycle of the friends’ speeches has run its course.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu describes the friends as dumbfounded, perhaps speaking of them to Job or to onlookers. They observe that the friends’ silence leaves room for a new voice, and that the book will later bring the LORD’s voice after Elihu’s.

verses.text: Shall I wait, because they don’t speak, because they stand still, and answer no more?
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu asks whether he should wait because the others do not speak and stand still. Arminian readers note that Elihu sees their silence as an obligation for him to speak, and they hear in the question an urgency that comes from wanting the conversation to reach a conclusion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu treats the silence of the elders as permission to speak. They observe that readers differ on whether his decision shows courage in the face of a stalled debate or impatience, and they do not settle the matter for the reader.

verses.text: I also will answer my part, and I also will show my opinion.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “I also will answer my part, and I also will show my opinion.” Arminian readers note that Elihu sees himself as having a part to play in the dialogue, and they read the repetition of his intention as emphasis on his readiness to contribute what the others have not.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repeated phrase from 32:10 and the stress on I also. They read the verse as Elihu insisting on his right to be heard, and they observe that both his supporters and his critics among interpreters have found this insistence significant for how they read him.

verses.text: For I am full of words. The spirit within me constrains me.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “For I am full of words. The spirit within me constrains me.” Arminian readers note that Elihu describes an inner compulsion to speak, which some take as a sense of being moved by God and others as simply the pressure of pent-up words; they hold both readings open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the word rendered spirit here can also mean breath, as in 32:8, and that the verse can be read as a claim to divine prompting or as a vivid description of an eager speaker. They do not decide between these readings.

verses.text: Behold, my breast is as wine which has no vent; like new wineskins it is ready to burst.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says his breast is like wine with no vent, like new wineskins ready to burst. Arminian readers note the vivid image of fermenting wine straining its container, and they see Elihu conveying how difficult it has been to keep silent while the older men spoke.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image and observe that some interpreters hear in it a touch of humor or self-importance, while others see sincere urgency. They read the verse as part of Elihu’s long preface, which readers evaluate in different ways.

verses.text: I will speak, that I may be refreshed. I will open my lips and answer.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “I will speak, that I may be refreshed. I will open my lips and answer.” Arminian readers note that Elihu expects relief from speaking, and they observe that his motive includes both a desire to help Job and a personal need to release what he has held back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu’s stated motive is partly personal relief. They observe that this candor may be read sympathetically or critically, and they hold that the worth of his speech depends on its content rather than on his reasons for giving it.

verses.text: Please don’t let me respect any man’s person, neither will I give flattering titles to any man.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, “Please don’t let me respect any man’s person, neither will I give flattering titles to any man.” Arminian readers note that Elihu commits himself to impartiality, a value the wisdom books and the law commend, and they see a resolve to speak truth regardless of status.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that impartiality is a virtue both traditions affirm, and that Job himself warned the friends against showing partiality for God (13:8, 10). They read Elihu’s promise as a standard by which his own speech may also be measured.

verses.text: For I don’t know how to give flattering titles, or else my Maker would soon take me away.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says he does not know how to flatter, “or else my Maker would soon take me away.” Arminian readers note that Elihu speaks with a sense of accountability to God as his Maker, and they see in this a reminder that speech about God and to others is answerable to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu grounds his honesty in the fear of his Maker, a motive both traditions affirm. They observe that the reference to his Maker anticipates 33:4 and 33:6, where Elihu speaks of being made by the Spirit of God and formed from clay.
